When simplifying a linear expression, our goal is to combine like terms so that the expression has fewer terms and is easier to work with.

Content:

items.readable_text:
Content:
Sometimes, like terms are not written next to each other. In these cases, we first rearrange the expression so that like terms are grouped together, and then we combine them.

Content:
For example, consider the expression [MATH: 12r - 5 + 3r.] The two variable terms, [MATH: 12r] and [MATH: 3r,] are like terms, but they are separated by a constant.

Content:
We can rewrite the expression so that the like terms are together:

Content:
[MATH: 12r − 5 + 3r|=; 12r + 3r_(⏟)_(rterms) − 5]

Content:
Now that the like terms are grouped, we combine them by adding their coefficients:

Content:
[MATH: 12r + 3r_(⏟) − 5|=; (12 + 3)r − 5|=; 15r − 5]

Content:
Rearranging terms makes it easier to see which terms can be combined before simplifying the expression.

items.readable_text:
Content:
Some linear expressions contain terms with different variables. Even though these terms may look similar, they are not like terms and cannot be combined with each other.

Content:
For example, consider the expression [MATH: 6x - 2x + 5y + y.] The [MATH: x] terms and the [MATH: y] terms represent different quantities, so they must be combined separately.

Content:
[MATH: 6x − 2x + 5y + y|=; 6x − 2x_(⏟)_(xterms) + 5y + y_(⏟)_(yterms)]

Content:
We now combine each group of like terms:

Content:
[MATH: 6x − 2x_(⏟)_() + 5y + y_(⏟)_()|=; (6 − 2)x + (5 + 1)y|=; 4x + 6y]

Content:
When simplifying expressions with more than one variable, always group and combine like terms one variable at a time.

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
When simplifying a linear expression, our goal is to combine like terms so that the expression has fewer terms and is easier to work with.

Content:
Recall that like terms are terms that have the same variable part. Because the variable parts represent the same quantity, the terms can be added or subtracted.

Content:
For example, consider the expression [MATH: 8x - 3x.] The terms [MATH: 8x] and [MATH: -3x] are like terms, so we can combine them by adding their coefficients:

Content:
[MATH: 8x − 3x|=; (8 − 3)_(⏟)_(coefficients)x|=; 5x]

Content:
When combining like terms:

Content:
- add the coefficients if the terms are being added, and
- subtract the coefficients if one term is being subtracted.

Content:
In this lesson, you will practice simplifying expressions by combining like terms step by step.

Content:
Sometimes, a term may appear without a written number in front of the variable. For example, [MATH: x] means we are adding [MATH: 1x,] and [MATH: -x] means we are subtracting [MATH: 1x.]

---

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
We have two like terms, [MATH: 9x] and [MATH: -4x.]

To collect these like terms, we combine them into a single term by subtracting their coefficients:

[MATH: 9x − 4x|=; (9 − 4)x|=; 5x]

Item 8 — Tutorial: Rearranging Terms to Group Like Terms

Content:
Sometimes, like terms are not written next to each other. In these cases, we first rearrange the expression so that like terms are grouped together, and then we combine them.

Content:
For example, consider the expression [MATH: 12r - 5 + 3r.] The two variable terms, [MATH: 12r] and [MATH: 3r,] are like terms, but they are separated by a constant.

Content:
We can rewrite the expression so that the like terms are together:

Content:
[MATH: 12r − 5 + 3r|=; 12r + 3r_(⏟)_(rterms) − 5]

Content:
Now that the like terms are grouped, we combine them by adding their coefficients:

Content:
[MATH: 12r + 3r_(⏟) − 5|=; (12 + 3)r − 5|=; 15r − 5]

Content:
Rearranging terms makes it easier to see which terms can be combined before simplifying the expression.

---

EXPLANATION

Explanation:
We rearrange the terms so that the like terms, [MATH: 14m] and [MATH: -5m,] are together.

[MATH: \eqalign{
14m - 6 - 5m &= \[5pt]
\underbrace{14m - 5m}_{m \textrm{ terms}} - 6 &
}]

Then, we combine the like terms:

[MATH: \eqalign{
\underbrace{14m - 5m} - 6 &= \[5pt]
(14 - 5)m - 6 &= \[5pt]
9m - 6
}]

Item 12 — Tutorial: Simplifying Expressions with More Than One Variable

Content:
Some linear expressions contain terms with different variables. Even though these terms may look similar, they are not like terms and cannot be combined with each other.

Content:
For example, consider the expression [MATH: 6x - 2x + 5y + y.] The [MATH: x] terms and the [MATH: y] terms represent different quantities, so they must be combined separately.

Content:
[MATH: 6x − 2x + 5y + y|=; 6x − 2x_(⏟)_(xterms) + 5y + y_(⏟)_(yterms)]

Content:
We now combine each group of like terms:

Content:
[MATH: 6x − 2x_(⏟)_() + 5y + y_(⏟)_()|=; (6 − 2)x + (5 + 1)y|=; 4x + 6y]

Content:
When simplifying expressions with more than one variable, always group and combine like terms one variable at a time.

---

Item 13 — Example: Combining Multiple Groups of Like Terms

Example Prompt:
[MATH: 4m + 3m + 6n - 2n - 5 =]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
We have two groups of two like terms, [MATH: 4m] and [MATH: 3m,] and [MATH: 6n] and [MATH: -2n.]

To collect these like terms, we combine each group into a single term, adding their coefficients:

[MATH: \eqalign{
\underbrace{4m + 3m}_{m \textrm{ terms}}\,+\, \underbrace{6n - 2n}_{n \textrm{ terms}} - 5 &= \[5pt]
(4+3)m + (6 - 2)n - 5 &= \[5pt]
7m + 4n - 5
}]
